prompt: Match each flagged value to the kind of outlier it is.
hint: Real or not? Same population or not?

pairs.left: A restaurant ordering 80 kg of tomatoes from a household grocer

prompt: What should happen to a value that is real and belongs to the population being described, however extreme?
hint: Is it part of what you are describing?

choices.text: Remove it so the mean is representative
choices.why: Removing real members of the population describes a different, tidier population that does not exist.

choices.text: Keep it
choices.why: Right. A genuine extreme is part of what is being described, as the founder's salary is part of the payroll.

choices.text: Replace it with the median
choices.why: That invents a value nobody recorded.

choices.text: Move it into a separate table and forget it
choices.why: Separating is for values from another population; this one belongs here.

prompt: Q1 is 30 and Q3 is 42. Where is the lower fence of the 1.5 IQR rule?
The IQR rule flags 17 of Horta's 400 baskets. What is the most reasonable reading?
hint: Does the rule judge, or point?

choices.text: Seventeen recording errors to delete
choices.why: Nothing says they are errors; the rule flags, it does not judge.

choices.text: Proof that the data is not normal, so the rule is useless
choices.why: The rule is still useful as a list of things to look at, whatever the shape.

choices.text: A sign that the fences should be moved until none is flagged
choices.why: Moving the rule to get the answer you want is the opposite of checking.

choices.text: A list to check; on skewed data most will be real
choices.why: Right. On a long right tail the rule flags real big shops by design; checking decides which, if any, are wrong.

prompt: Why do outliers have little effect on the fences of the IQR rule?
hint: What are the fences made of?

choices.text: They are built from quartiles, which ignore the extremes
choices.why: Right. The quartiles are robust, so the values being hunted cannot drag the fences towards themselves.

choices.text: The fences are fixed in advance at 1.5
choices.why: 1.5 is the multiplier; the fences also depend on the quartiles of the data.

choices.text: Outliers are removed before the quartiles are computed
choices.why: Nothing is removed; the quartiles simply do not depend on the extremes.

choices.text: The rule only works on normal data
choices.why: That is a different point, and an overstatement; robustness is what protects the fences.

prompt: In a sample of n values no z-score can exceed (n − 1) ÷ √n. What is that ceiling for n = 10? Give two decimal places.
With two typos among the twelve baskets, their z-scores are 2.52 and 1.69, and a z > 3 rule flags neither. What is this called?

choices.text: Winsorising
choices.why: Winsorising caps extreme values; this is about a rule failing to see them.

choices.text: Overdispersion
choices.why: That is a variance above a Poisson's mean, from lesson 8.

choices.text: Masking
choices.why: Right. Each error inflates the standard deviation enough to hide the other.

choices.text: Regression to the mean
choices.why: Not related: that is about repeated measurements drifting back towards the average.

prompt: A colleague runs a z > 3 rule on 10 delivery times and reports 'no outliers'. What should you say?
hint: What is the largest z ten values can produce?

choices.text: Good: the data is clean
choices.why: With ten values the rule could not have flagged anything, so its silence proves nothing.

choices.text: Lower the threshold to z > 2 to be safe
choices.why: That still suffers from masking; a robust rule fixes the cause.

choices.text: With ten values no z gets past 2.85, so it never fires
choices.why: Right. The ceiling (n − 1) ÷ √n is 2.85 for ten values; a robust z-score or the IQR rule is needed.

choices.text: The rule needs at least 30 values to give any result
choices.why: Thirty is not the issue; the ceiling on z is, and it rises slowly with n.

prompt: Values 10, 12, 13, 15 and 40 have median 13. What is their MAD?
For those values, median 13 and MAD 2, what is the modified z-score of 40, 0.6745 × (40 − 13) ÷ 2? Give two decimal places.
Why does the modified z-score find the two typos that the ordinary z-score missed?
hint: What are its centre and its spread?

choices.text: Median and MAD are not pulled by the typos
choices.why: Right. The yardstick stays the size of the ordinary values, so the errors stand out by dozens of units.

choices.text: It uses a lower threshold
choices.why: Its threshold, 3.5, is higher; the difference is in the ingredients.

choices.text: It removes the largest value before measuring
choices.why: Nothing is removed; robust ingredients simply ignore extremes.

choices.text: It multiplies by 0.6745, which enlarges the errors
choices.why: 0.6745 is less than 1 and only aligns the scale with the ordinary z on normal data.

prompt: The median of the distances from the median is called the median absolute ___, or MAD.
Put these questions about a flagged value in the order this lesson asks them.
hint: From the cheapest check to the one that needs a decision.
items: Does the rest of its row agree with it?
Does it belong to the population being described?

prompt: A R$ 2,126.00 basket holds three items. What does that suggest?
hint: Does the row agree with itself?

choices.text: A genuine big shop
choices.why: Three items for over R$ 2,000 at a grocer is hard to believe; big shops have many items.

choices.text: A restaurant customer
choices.why: A restaurant's order would also have many items.

choices.text: Nothing, since items and price are unrelated
choices.why: At a grocer, more items mean a larger basket; that relation is the evidence.

choices.text: Probably a mistake in the value
choices.why: Right. The row disagrees with itself; the payment record will settle it.

prompt: Five flagged deliveries all come from the same courier on the same Tuesday. What is the most useful next step?
hint: What do the five have in common?

choices.text: Delete the five as outliers
choices.why: A pattern points at a cause; deleting hides it.

choices.text: Look for a common cause that day
choices.why: Right. A broken scanner, a road closure or a new phone app: the pattern is the finding.

choices.text: Treat each one separately with the z-score rule
choices.why: Treating them separately misses what they have in common.

choices.text: Report the mean without that courier
choices.why: That drops a courier without knowing why their day was unusual.

prompt: Values 20, 30, 40, 50 and 200 are winsorised by capping anything above 60 at 60. What is the new mean?
The mean basket is R$ 82.78 with every order and R$ 74.38 without the 17 beyond the fence. What is the honest report?
hint: Which version tells the reader most?

choices.text: R$ 74.38, since outliers distort the mean
choices.why: The 17 are real orders; reporting only the lower figure hides real revenue.

choices.text: Both, naming the 17 orders that make the difference
choices.why: Right. A sensitivity analysis shows how much the conclusion depends on the extremes.

choices.text: The average of the two figures
choices.why: Averaging two summaries answers no question anyone asked.

choices.text: R$ 82.78 alone; the outliers are real
choices.why: Keeping them is right, but the reader should know the figure leans on a handful of orders.

prompt: An analyst removes three outliers, the result becomes significant, and nothing is written down. What is the main problem?
hint: What does the written record protect against?

choices.text: Three is too many outliers to remove
choices.why: The number is not the issue; the missing record and the timing are.

choices.text: Outliers can never be removed
choices.why: Mistakes and values from another population can be removed, with the reason recorded.

choices.text: The z-score rule should have been used instead
choices.why: The rule used to flag them is secondary to what was done afterwards.

choices.text: Nobody can tell whether they went because the result looked better
choices.why: Right. A decision made after seeing the result, and not recorded, cannot be told apart from cherry-picking.
